extracted.intended_audience: members of the Royal Society; experimental natural philosophers and observational astronomers (17th-century scientists)
extracted.subtask_description: Designing, performing, and reporting natural-philosophy experiments (atmospheric/fluids experiments) and observational astronomy (satellite/planet discovery) with attention to controls, instrument choice, repeated observation, and interpretation of competing hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poising and selection of glass-bubbles for atmospheric weight tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Poise several small glass-bubbles in water, each with a short slender stem so that very small changes of weight will make them either emerge or sink; trial several and choose the fittest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is difficult to poise several bubbles precisely; therefore it is not strange that they do not all rise and fall together. It is not amiss to poise a greater number together so that, after trial made of all, the fittest may be chosen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish thermal buoyancy from atmospheric-weight effects
rubrics_metrics.description: When bubbles change position, determine whether cause is rarefaction/condensation of the included air (temperature effects) or a change in the weight/pressure of the ambient atmosphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heating (sun beams, ambient heat) rarefies air inside bubbles and can drive out water causing rise; cooling causes condensation and sinking (commonly at night). Distinguish these from motions due to varying atmospheric weight by consulting a baroscope (barometer) — bubble posture can predict whether mercury will be high or low.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use barometer readings to verify atmospheric-weight hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Consult the baroscope to see whether the atmosphere is 'so heavy or so light, that [the bubbles] ought to' rise or fall; compare bubble motion with mercury levels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author reports having, divers times, predicted whether the mercury in the baroscope would be high or low by observing the situation and posture of the bubbles; consulting the instrument verified conjectures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control for imbibition/adsorption confounders in bubble experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for the phenomenon that a bubble which floated may afterwards subside or remain at bottom even after the apparent cause is removed, possibly due to imbibition of aerial particles by the water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This difficult phenomenon should be considered a separate subject of inquiry; when observed, note it as a confounder rather than attributing the effect to atmospheric-weight changes alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation principle: atmosphere acts as an incumbent heavy body on water
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for the fact that the atmosphere, though a much lighter fluid, leans or presses upon the water and thereby can operate upon bodies under water to produce sinking or emersion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The experiments mentioned are used to confirm the idea that the atmosphere is incumbent as a heavy body upon the terraqueous globe and acts by pressure transmitted through water.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminology and hypothesis caution about vacuity in Torricellian experiment
rubrics_metrics.description: When discussing vacuity created by Torricellian and similar experiments, avoid asserting absolute vacuity; be explicit about what is meant by 'air' (heterogeneous mixture, purer aether, materia subtilis, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author expressly cautions not to be understood as affirming absolute vacuity, and suggests distinguishing between the heterogeneous air we breathe and any purer aether or materia subtilis invoked by other authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider alternative hypotheses: subtile matter percolation vs spring/elasticity of air
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess explanations that attribute anomalous Torricellian heights to (a) a subtile matter that penetrates glass/quicksilver, or (b) the spring/elasticity in the air (and lack thereof in quicksilver), or (c) a mixture of heterogeneous air parts with different properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a subtile matter would balance itself as common air does, whether percolation through glass explains sudden falls, and whether sudden falls indicate the action of spring/elastic force rather than slow percolative motion. Consider plausibility of each and recommend experiment to adjudicate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate role of cohesion/adhesion of quicksilver to glass in Torricellian behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine whether cohesion of quicksilver parts or adhesion to glass is responsible for standing higher than ordinary standard; consider whether quicksilver adheres to glass or rather declines contact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author argues quicksilver is not apt to stick to glass (visible to the eye) and so separation forces between quicksilver and glass are unlikely to explain the effect; cohesion between quicksilver parts may be less relevant since liquid can slide down sides.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis: spring/elasticity of air vs lack in quicksilver
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider that air possesses a spring or elasticity which may impart motion (pulsion/percussion) to heavy bodies, whereas water or purified quicksilver may lack such spring, explaining why they may remain suspended until a perturbing force acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If matter at rest continues till put in motion by force, that force may be percussion (shaking) or pulsion (expansion of adjacent springy parts). The sudden fall of quicksilver upon concussion supports the spring explanation over percolation alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experiment 1: large low tube (<29 in) top-full with small hole — sinking behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: Test whether a large low tube of less height than the common standard (about 29 inches) filled top-full of quicksilver and provided with a small hole at the top will stand top-full or will sink, and if it sinks, whether it does so slowly with a hissing noise or falls suddenly and silently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This was a specific experiment hinted by Lord Brouncker and recommended to be tried by those with suitable apparatus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experiment 2: adhesion test with polished marbles/metal plates in exhausted receiver
rubrics_metrics.description: Test whether two polished marbles or metalline plates will stick to one another longer in an exhausted receiver than is accounted for by ordinary counterbalance in the Torricellian experiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeat the experiment despite prior intimations; if plates stick longer, it may proceed from want of elastic power between the plates to force them asunder, suggesting spirituous vapours are not springy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experiment 3: syphon of unequal legs in exhausted receiver
rubrics_metrics.description: Try whether a syphon with unequal legs will run in an exhausted receiver with water or quicksilver to a greater height than is accountable for by ordinary theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If it succeeds, the author takes this to proceed from the spring of the little remaining air in the receiver; the experiment is worth repeating even if previously tried by Huygens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experiment 4: long tube submerged so less above level — lifting behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: Test whether a tube of greater length than 29 inches but so immersed that its top is less than 29 inches above the external level might, if filled with well-cleansed quicksilver, be gently lifted with the quicksilver in it not only to the ordinary standard but to higher heights (H or D).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalent but alternative approaches (see experiments 5 and 8) are suggested to decide the question of spring vs percolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experiment 5: inclined tube gradually erected to remain full above standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Fill a long tube with cleansed quicksilver when it is inclined so its apparent height above ambient level is less than 29 inches, then gently erect it; observe whether it may remain full up to heights greater than the usual standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an easier administration of experiment 4 and tests whether quicksilver can be made to stand top-full higher than ordinary by slow erection rather than violent perturbation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experiment 6: syphon test in open air — cleansed quicksilver run height
rubrics_metrics.description: Test whether cleansed quicksilver will, in the open air, run in a syphon higher than 29 inches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If not in air, see experiment 7 (lower leg opening into well-cleansed water). This probes whether the medium into which the lower leg opens affects maximum syphon height.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experiment 7: syphon test with lower leg opening into cleansed water
rubrics_metrics.description: If cleansed quicksilver does not run higher than 29 inches in air, test whether it will do so if the lower leg opens into well-cleansed water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This variation discriminates whether the surrounding medium (air vs cleansed water) impacts the maximum syphon height achievable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experiment 8: partial voiding and stoppage test for sustained suspension
rubrics_metrics.description: In a tube filled with cleansed quicksilver standing top-full at greater height than usual, force out some part (not by air admission but by jogging the tube) and immediately stop it; test whether the remaining column at greater height than the usual standard will stand by itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If it succeeds, it indicates want of a spring to put quicksilver in motion rather than lack of room for subtile matter recollection; if it fails, then springy air penetrating the quicksilver is more plausible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experiment 9: suspension with orifice not immersed
rubrics_metrics.description: Test whether cleansed quicksilver will remain suspended in an inverted tube (even a short one with small orifice) whose orifice is not immersed in quicksilver but exposed to open air or placed in water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If it will, follow with experiment 10 to test persistence when a little is forced out leaving a void at the top.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experiment 10: small void at top after forcing out some quicksilver
rubrics_metrics.description: If suspension in experiment 9 is observed, test whether permitting a small amount to be forced out leaving some void room at the top will still allow the remaining quicksilver to remain suspended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explores the sensitivity of suspension to small voids and helps discriminate between competing mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observational criterion: identify new planet by motion relative to fixed stars and Saturn
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify candidate planets/satellites by observing motion relative to fixed stars and comparing relative positions to Saturn and known satellites across multiple dates to detect systematic digressions (westward/eastward) and relative distance changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare observations with fixed stars and Saturn's ordinary satellite; a true planet shows manifest motion relative to fixed stars and characteristic changes in distance from Saturn (e.g., increasing westward then decreasing) that allow inference about whether it is a satellite and about its orbital phase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use repeated, collaborative observations with suitable telescopes
rubrics_metrics.description: Observe candidate objects on multiple dates, preferably with long-focus telescopes (examples: 17, 20, 35 feet), and corroborate sightings with other observers (Huygens, Picard, Mariotte, Romer, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weather limits observation windows; use the best available telescopes and corroborate to improve confidence; initial discovery may be by a 17-foot instrument, while longer (35-foot) instruments help refine positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infer orbital period and semidiameter from successive position/time measurements
rubrics_metrics.description: Deduce the period by noting return-to-position intervals and counting revolutions between observations; estimate semidiameter relative to Saturn's ring and use proportions (Keplerian relations) to relate period and distance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: combining observations led to judgment that the interior satellite's revolution is 4.5 days and that the semidiameter of its circle is three and a quarter semidia of Saturn's ring; careful combination of observations can exclude shorter period hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement techniques: time-difference and latitude measures, and ephemeris construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure distances/positions both by eye-estimate and by measuring the time between the planet's passage and that of Saturn's centre; note latitudes relative to a reference line (e.g., 'line of his wings') and compile an ephemeris from combined data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early distance estimates may be by eye; refined measures use timing of passages; noting observed latitudes (southern/northern) in particular semicircles aids orbit characterization; produce ephemeris to predict future positions until observational constraints (e.g., solar occultation) intervene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for observational limitations and interpret gaps cautiously
rubrics_metrics.description: When weather or solar glare prevents continued observation, interpret absences and apparent changes cautiously; avoid over-interpreting single-night positions without sequence data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors repeatedly note weather prevented observation; differences between appearances (east/west, latitude) require multiple corroborating nights to determine whether apparent changes are due to orbital motion or observational error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine multiple methods (visual estimate, timing, instrument comparison) to strengthen claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a combination of eye estimates, timing methods, and observations from different telescopes/observers to arrive at robust determinations about new satellites/planets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Initial detections might come from a 17-foot telescope by Campani; subsequent verification and measurement used 20- and 35-foot telescopes and multiple observers to produce consistent ephemeris and period estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report uncertainties and alternative interpretations honestly
rubrics_metrics.description: When multiple explanations exist (e.g., subtile matter penetration, springy air, percolation, adhesion effects), report the merits and difficulties of each and recommend experiments rather than prejudging the outcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author refrains from dogmatic conclusions and suggests that experiments (many listed) are the best way to settle the question; he explicitly declines to pre-judge and requests that appropriate experiments be performed by those better equipped.
